newsitem.title: NORWAY: Braathens profits rise, but costs too.
newsitem.headline: Braathens profits rise, but costs too.

text.p: Norwegian airliner Braathens SAFE, which is increasingly competing for airspace with big brother Scandinavian Airlines System, said on Wednesday first-quarter net profits soared 120 percent to 44 million crowns.
But while operating revenues rose by seven percent to 1.04 billion crowns from the corresponding 1996 period, operating costs increased by 12 percent to 960 million crowns.
"It is not satisfactory that costs in the first quarter are growing more than revenue at a time when we stand before tougher competition," Managing Director Erik Braathen said in a statement.
The carrier blamed the cost increase on salary raises and higher fuel prices.

"Immediate measures for controlling the sharp increase in personnel expenses will be evaluated," the statement said. "Simplified distribution and more efficient maintenance of aircraft and engines should impact the figures beginning in 1998."

Last month Braathens, Finland's Finnair and domestic Swedish carrier Transwede Airways announced plans to increase co-operation in a move seen as an attack on SAS (SAS) SASb.CO domination of the region.
Braathens owns half of Transwede and holds an option to buy the remaining 50 percent before the end of this year.
SAS said on Tuesday that increasing competition in its home territory plunged it into a 269 million Swedish crown pre-tax loss in the first quarter of 1997.
Braathens last November launched regular flights between Oslo and Stockholm and has said it plans a further offensive in the region including a frequent-flyer programme linked to British Airways.

Mainly because of a new Stockholm route, revenue from international routes increased to 89 million crowns from 64 million. Net expenses linked to the Stockholm run were about 17 million crowns for the first quarter, Braathens said.

The number of passengers on Norwegian routes increased by 1.5 percent from the first quarter last year. The passenger load factor on Norwegian routes increased to 53.2 percent from 48.8 percent, which means planes were more than half-full. The figure for international routes was unchanged at 45 percent.
The carrier operated 25 aircraft in the first quarter, one more than in the corresponding period in 1996.
